doc.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How experiences shaped his evolution
summary: Playing differently with each person; Monk and Tatum.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you have an experience playing, whether it’s one concert or a tour or… with somebody that you, you know, haven’t been working with before, do you find anything particular in your mindset when you… that says, “Oh, well, you know, next time I do this, I might do it differently?” Or did it… ‘cause you are constantly evolving, and I’m wondering if you have any sense of how different musical experiences…
Or if that’s something that’s too intangible.

No. Well, I think, I hope I’ve in different ways talked about it quite a bit in the last couple of days. Yeah, it does. And as I said, the same as just conversations, like my conversation with you. You react to different situations differently according to people and… especially when you’re, you’re in a improvisatory art form kind of a… But I’m sure even classical musicians play differently even though the music is written with different accompanists and accomplices and orchestras and stuff so… Yeah, it’s a very… in a good sense, it’s a very human experience. And I mentioned working with… duets with Bill Evans and what great fun that was. And I’m sure… I never got to play with Thelonious Monk but I’m sure that would have been different. I wish I had. Even in a duet, you know. Art Tatum, I’m sure he would fill in all the… (laughs) all the empty spaces. So I would just sorta sit there and smile. But he wouldn’t see me so… Yeah, I told you, that was funny about Dave MacKay, also… being blind.
